timeline.description: Engineer Richard Friedmann builds Ebro into a leading manufacturer of patented horsehair upholstery and a key partner of the automobile industry.
timeline.longDescription: Ebro – an acronym of Erste Berliner Dampf-Rosshaarspinnerei [First Steam Horsehair Spinning Mill, Berlin] – was established around 1900 by engineer Richard Friedmann as a wholesale company for upholstery materials. He soon began manufacturing his own supplies and in 1924 the factory became a stock corporation, with his youngest brother Ernst as partner and shareholder. The factory premises stood on opposite sides of Pistorius Strasse (66-69 and 95-96) in Berlin-Weissensee. Ebro manufactured upholstery units made with horsehair by a special patented technique used by only two other German factories, and became an important partner of the growing automobile industry – 1936 business records list Auto-Union, Daimler Benz, Adam Opel and Bayerische Motorenwerke among its major clients.

timeline.description: Classified a priority business 'for German interests', Ebro attracts the attention of Nazi economic advisor Heinrich Hunke, who pressures the owners to sell.
timeline.longDescription: In the years after 1933, Ebro was classified as a priority business for the German Reich and deemed significant 'for German interests' in an assessment by the Reichskreditgesellschaft bank. From 1936 onwards, Heinrich Hunke – economic advisor to the Berlin Nazi Party since 1928 – increased the pressure on the company's Jewish shareholders to hand over their factory. They put up considerable resistance and 'sales' negotiations proceeded only very slowly. As late as 1937, Richard Friedmann tried to avert the hostile takeover by appointing a brother-in-law who was a Nazi Party member to the board of directors.

timeline.description: Terrorised and intimidated, the Friedmanns are forced out. Hunke secures the factory for a give-away price of 375,000 Reich marks.
timeline.longDescription: In 1938, Hunke pushed the takeover by increasingly drastic means. He effected the immediate transfer of Richard Friedmann's 75 per cent shareholding to his own non-Jewish wife Ella, the shares held on trust by lawyer Dr. Erich Naue. Ernst Friedmann was forced to leave the business, and an SS officer took his place on the board. Before being finally ousted in July 1938, Richard Friedmann had to train the new managers, who left Der Stürmer on his desk each morning with anti-Semitic articles underlined in red; one morning he found 'Clear out Jew' daubed in huge red letters on the factory wall. The 61-year-old managing director never set foot in his company again. Threatened with expropriation and the destruction of the factory, the owners caved in in late June 1938. Despite bidders offering up to 900,000 Reich marks, Hunke secured the factory for 375,000 – covered by the business' own surplus profit. The Friedmanns had no access to the money.

timeline.description: The Friedmann brothers are deported or driven to death. After the war, Ebro is nationalized in the GDR and finally restored to Ella Friedmann in 1952.
timeline.longDescription: The Friedmann brothers remained in Germany after the company's seizure. On November 1, 1941, 61-year-old Ernst Friedmann was deported to the Litzmannstadt (Lodz) ghetto together with his brother Kurt, who died there on March 15, 1942; on May 9, 1942, Ernst was deported to the Kulmhof (Chelmno) extermination camp. Anticipating his own imminent deportation after being summoned to the local police station, Richard Friedmann committed suicide at home on July 16, 1942, aged 65. In farewell letters he wrote: 'I am not willing to let myself be tortured for a long time in a concentration camp.'

timeline.description: Ebro is nationalized in the GDR and restored to Ella Friedmann in 1952. Today little remains of the former premises on Pistorius Strasse.
timeline.longDescription:
After the end of the Second World War in 1945, the main shareholders Naue and Hunke lost interest in the factory. Categorized as 'ownerless' by the Soviet military administration, Ebro was placed under trusteeship in 1945 and eventually nationalized by the GDR in 1949; on May 30, 1949, the company was deleted from Berlin's commercial register. However, Ebro continued to exist in West Berlin as a number of bank-held securities remained unaffected by expropriation in the GDR. In 1952, the company was officially restored to Ella Friedmann (née Kunze, 1882-1974), who registered for liquidation the same year. Once wealthy, after 1945 she received a pension of only 200 DM a month.

The site today

Today, little remains of the former Ebro premises on one side of Pistorius Strasse in Weissensee. A supermarket has been built on the opposite side.
